faq.a: Irritation of the diaphragm transmits via the phrenic nerve (C3‑C5) to the shoulder tip.
faq.q: Why is pain referred to the shoulder in a ruptured spleen?

faq.a: Shifting dullness: fluid moves to the dependent flank, making it dull, while the opposite flank becomes resonant.
faq.q: What bedside sign suggests ascites when ultrasound is unavailable?

faq.a: Perforated ulcer gives sudden, severe epigastric pain with rigid abdomen and free air on X‑ray; pancreatitis shows epigastric pain radiating to the back, often with elevated enzymes.
faq.q: How can you differentiate between a perforated ulcer and acute pancreatitis?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with right upper quadrant pain and fever – what is your next bedside step and why? — Assess for Murphy’s sign; positive sign points to acute cholecystitis, prompting early imaging or surgical referral.

A patient with sickle cell disease has sudden left lower quadrant pain and guarding – which organ is most likely involved and what is the urgent management? — Suspect splenic sequestration; give urgent blood transfusion and monitor hemodynamics.

During a trauma assessment you find a rigid abdomen but no external wounds – what does this indicate and what immediate action is required? — Suggests intra‑abdominal bleeding or perforation; arrange rapid transfer to surgery.
How does the pattern of referred pain help you locate a duodenal ulcer? — Epigastric pain radiating to the back (T10‑T12) points to posterior duodenum, guiding endoscopic evaluation.

Explain why a patient with portal hypertension may develop ascites and how you would confirm it without ultrasound. — Increased hydrostatic pressure forces fluid into peritoneal cavity; confirm by shifting dullness and fluid wave test.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area presents with abdominal distension and hepatomegaly – what tropical disease should be considered and what key lab test supports it? — Consider hepatic schistosomiasis; eosinophilia and stool ova detection support diagnosis.

Why is the inferior mesenteric artery ligated in a left hemicolectomy and what collateral circulation protects the colon? — Ligation removes blood supply to diseased segment; the marginal artery of Drummond provides collateral flow.
What clinical feature distinguishes peritoneal irritation from simple abdominal tenderness? — Presence of rebound tenderness or guarding indicates peritoneal irritation.
ai.title: Essential Abdominal Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Key structures of the abdomen, their relationships, blood and nerve supply, and common clinical implications for low‑resource settings. Focuses on bedside relevance for ward rounds and exams.

b: Four quadrants and nine regions divide the abdomen for localisation.
Peritoneal layers create a potential space for fluid and infection.
sections.p: The abdomen houses the gastrointestinal tract, solid organs, major vessels and nerves. Understanding its layout guides diagnosis of pain, masses and organ dysfunction.

b: Rectus abdominis runs vertically within the rectus sheath.
Posterior abdominal wall contains psoas, quadratus lumborum and kidneys.
sections.p: From superficial to deep: skin → superficial fascia → muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) → transversalis fascia → peritoneum.

b: The liver lies under the right rib cage, protected by the diaphragm.
The spleen is tucked under the left 9th‑11th ribs.
sections.p: Anteriorly the abdominal wall overlies the peritoneal cavity; posteriorly it contacts the vertebral column and retroperitoneal structures.

b: Celiac trunk supplies foregut organs (stomach, liver, spleen).
Superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut (small intestine, right colon).
Inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut (left colon, rectum).
sections.p: Arterial inflow is from the abdominal aorta and its branches; venous drainage follows the portal and systemic systems.

b: Visceral pain from the foregut is referred to the epigastrium (T5‑T9).
Midgut pain refers to periumbilical region (T10‑T12).
sections.p: Somatic innervation comes from lower thoracic (T7‑T12) intercostal nerves; autonomic supply is via the vagus (parasympathetic) and sympathetic lumbar splanchnic nerves.

b: Peristalsis moves contents through the gut.
The liver detoxifies blood and produces clotting factors.
sections.p: The abdomen supports digestion, absorption, immune defence, and houses organs that regulate metabolism, fluid balance and hormone production.

b: Rigidity and guarding indicate an acute surgical abdomen.
sections.p: Abdominal pain localisation, palpable masses, and signs of peritonitis are core bedside skills. In low‑resource settings, imaging may be limited, so physical exam is vital.

t.b: Detects free fluid, organ enlargement or gallstones; if unavailable, use focused clinical exam and plain X‑ray.
Helps confirm pancreatitis; if not available, diagnose by pain pattern, vomiting and tender epigastrium.

b: Right upper quadrant pain → liver, gallbladder, duodenum.
Left lower quadrant pain → sigmoid colon, ovary, ureter.
sections.p: Remember the four quadrants, peritoneal signs, and vascular supply landmarks for quick differential diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent vomiting with inability to pass stool or gas
